messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
parts:
If a covariates is positive, x > 0, then the coefficients
for polynomials, say alpha1 x + alpha2 * x^{2}, become
strongly non-identified causing no end of fitting problems.
Unfortunately I’m trying to reproduce an existing analysis
that used such a polynomial so I can’t just get rid of the
higher-order terms.

Are there any tricks to decorrelate the coefficients by
transforming the covariates? The physicist in me wants
to do some kind of Gramm-Schmidt, but then that would
require a choice of kernel.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Identifying Polynomial Coefficients

On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:13:32 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
If a covariates is positive, x > 0, then the coefficients
for polynomials, say alpha1 x + alpha2 * x^{2}, become
strongly non-identified causing no end of fitting problems.
Unfortunately I’m trying to reproduce an existing analysis
that used such a polynomial so I can’t just get rid of the
higher-order terms.  

Are there any tricks to decorrelate the coefficients by
transforming the covariates?  The physicist in me wants
to do some kind of Gramm-Schmidt, but then that would
require a choice of kernel.

I have anecdotally observed (mostly from rstanarm) that orthogonal polynomials yield better sampling for the coefficients than raw polynomials. You can just type

poly

in R to see its source code, which uses a QR decomposition in the default case.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
parts:
On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:32:59 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Right, that’s what Gramm-Schmidt would yield, provided you
define a specific kernel.  Not sure which kernel would be best,
though.

Or is it going to be easier to just build everything into a design
matrix and do the QR explicitly?

We have an option to do the QR of a design matrix in rstanarm, and it seems to work well (but we haven't studied it that systematically). Basically you end up doing a GLM on Q instead of X = QR and then pre-multiply the resulting coefficients by the inverse of R to obtain the coefficients with respect to X as a generated quantity.

Ben

> On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:32:59 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:

Basically you end up doing a GLM on Q instead of X = QR and then pre-multiply the resulting coefficients by the inverse of R to obtain the coefficients with respect to X as a generated quantity.

Right. So instead of

y = normal( X* beta + alpha, sigma);

you’d fit

Q = qr_Q(X);
R = qr_R(X);
y = normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);

then

beta = mdivide_right_tri_low(beta_tilde, R); ?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
parts:
On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:45:21 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Right.  So instead of

y = normal( X* beta + alpha, sigma);

you’d fit

Q = qr_Q(X);
R = qr_R(X);
y = normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);

then

beta = mdivide_right_tri_low(beta_tilde, R); ?

Yeah, basically. We actually multiply Q by sqrt(N - 1) and divide R by sqrt(N - 1) to make beta_tilde have a more reasonable scale in large datasets. A lot of times ADVI only works well with this transformation.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
parts:
The dimensions are screwing with me here.

Let’s say that we have N data points and M covariates, where
N >> M.  In this case our original problem is

matrix[N, M] X; // data
vector[M] beta; // parameters
vector[N] alpha; // parameters
y ~ normal(X * beta + alpha, sigma);

If the covariates are highly correlated then this can cause
problems, so instead we want to use a QR decomposition,
to write

X * beta = (Q * R) * beta = Q * (R * beta) = Q * beta_tilde

and then fit the model

matrix[N, M] X; // data
matrix[N, N] Q;
matrix[N, M] R;
vector[N] beta_tilde; // parameters
vector[N] alpha; // parameters
y ~ normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);
beta = R \ beta_tilde;

But doesn't this replace the M original parameters with N >> M
new parameters?  Is the cost of decor relating really the
introduction of so many new parameters?

In any case qr_R is seg faulting on me so it looks like there
are bigger problems...
On Apr 8, 2016, at 5:00 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:45:21 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Right.  So instead of

y = normal( X* beta + alpha, sigma);

you’d fit

Q = qr_Q(X);
R = qr_R(X);
y = normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);

then

beta = mdivide_right_tri_low(beta_tilde, R); ?

Yeah, basically. We actually multiply Q by sqrt(N - 1) and divide R by sqrt(N - 1) to make beta_tilde have a more reasonable scale in large datasets. A lot of times ADVI only works well with this transformation.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
parts:
On Friday, April 15, 2016 at 5:44:04 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
matrix[N, M] X; // data
matrix[N, N] Q;
matrix[N, M] R;

In the "thin" QR decomposition of the "tall" NxM matrix X = Q * R, Q is supposed to be NxM and R is supposed to be MxM.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_decomposition#Rectangular_matrix
http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/classEigen_1_1HouseholderQR.html#a520fc76215d7722387a76e7b7a484ee0

Is Stan messing up? In rstanarm, we do the QR decomposition in R and don't pass in X.
vector[N] beta_tilde; // parameters

This should then be vector[M] beta_tilde.

Ben
